content: Penicillin G benzathine is a long-acting antibiotic used to treat a variety of bacterial infections. It is also employed to prevent certain bacterial infections, such as rheumatic fever. Always consult your healthcare provider for complete information about this medication and your specific health needs. This medication is administered via injection into a large muscle, as directed by your doctor. The dosage is determined based on your medical condition and response to treatment. If you are using this medication at home, ensure you are thoroughly trained by your healthcare provider on how to prepare and administer it. Avoid injecting it into or near an artery, nerve, or vein. Rotate the injection site each time to minimize muscle injury. Before use, visually inspect the product for particles or discoloration; do not use it if either is present. Continue the full course of treatment as prescribed, even if symptoms improve after a few days. Common side effects may include pain at the injection site, nausea, or vomiting. Remember, this medication has been prescribed because your doctor has determined that the benefits outweigh the risks of side effects. Rarely, this medication may cause a severe intestinal condition due to the bacteria Clostridioides difficile (C. difficile), which can occur during treatment or weeks to months after treatment has stopped. Prolonged or repeated use may lead to oral thrush or a new yeast infection. When used to treat syphilis or certain other infections, it may cause a reaction several hours after starting treatment, lasting up to 24 hours. Serious allergic reactions to this drug are rare but possible. Before using this medication, inform your doctor or pharmacist if you are allergic to it, other penicillins, cephalosporins, or any other substances. This product may contain inactive ingredients that could cause allergic reactions or other issues. Penicillin G benzathine may interfere with the effectiveness of live bacterial vaccines, such as the typhoid vaccine. During pregnancy, this medication should only be used when clearly needed. It passes into breast milk in small amounts. Drug interactions may alter how your medications work or increase the risk of serious side effects. Keep a list of all the products you use, including prescription and non-prescription drugs and herbal products, and share it with your doctor and pharmacist. This medication may interfere with certain lab tests, such as urine glucose tests, potentially causing false results. In the event of an overdose with serious symptoms like passing out or difficulty breathing, call emergency services (911 in the U.S.) immediately. Otherwise, contact a poison control center. U.S. residents can call 1-800-222-1222, and Canadian residents can call 1-844-764-7669. If you are using this medication for an extended period, your doctor may order lab tests, such as complete blood counts, kidney function tests, or blood cultures, to monitor your condition. It is crucial to receive each dose as scheduled. If you miss a dose, contact your doctor or pharmacist promptly for a new dosing schedule. Store this medication in the refrigerator or as directed by your pharmacist. Do not freeze it. Do not flush medications down the toilet or pour them into a drain unless instructed to do so. Properly discard this product when it is expired or no longer needed. Always consult your healthcare provider for complete and personalized medical advice.
